results.title: Yoda's hand and ear
results.brief_description:
Iconic, Yoda is. Small, funny and wise, he changed what a screen hero, or Jedi, could be. First appeared he did in Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back (1980), beloved through Frank Oz’s expressive performance.

Since then, in many forms Yoda has appeared: different puppets, a CGI character and, in Star Wars: The Last Jedi (2017), a version closer to his original puppet self. Strong with this one, the puppet is.

Designing Yoda

Yoda began with a simple brief: he needed to look very old, wise and not quite human. Early sketches made him more animal-like, but the design gradually settled on smaller, wrinkled and gnome-like. These drawings gave sculptors a starting point, but Yoda’s personality emerged through modelling, texture and masterful puppeteering. 

Head of make-up and creature effects Stuart Freeborn spent five months sculpting Yoda’s face. A photograph of Albert Einstein in the workshop inspired some of the wrinkles around Yoda’s eyes, though the final character also looked a lot like Freeborn himself. Yoda’s size was shaped around the length and width of puppeteer Frank Oz’s arm, so that Oz could perform the Jedi master from inside. David Barclay also joined Freeborn’s team, helping build Yoda before becoming one of his puppeteers.

Performing Yoda

Yoda’s power may come from the Force, but his character comes through performance. Frank Oz performed Yoda’s voice and main puppetry, bringing the wisdom, humour and impatience of the little Jedi master to life. David Barclay initially operated Yoda’s eyes, while other puppeteers controlled his ears and right hand. The ears were especially expressive, moved by cables that let them lift, droop or sharpen Yoda’s reactions.

Four Yoda puppets were made for Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back (1980). Nick Maley worked on all four, including a back-up puppet that ended up being used for most of Yoda’s scenes after the primary model often malfunctioned.  When Oz became unavailable for the final week of filming, he chose Barclay to take over Yoda’s main puppetry.

Rebuilding Yoda 

Decades after Star Wars: Episode V – The Empire Strikes Back (1980), Nick Maley returned to one of the puppets that defined his career. In 2016, he began reverse engineering a faithful rebuild of the back-up Yoda puppet he had helped create in 1979. The rebuild was completed in 2021. 

Maley now takes the rebuilt Yoda to speaking events, Comic Cons, schools and children’s hospitals, using the puppet to inspire new generations of makers, fans and storytellers. The project shows how screen puppetry depends on specialised craft that can easily be lost if it isn’t preserved and shared.

results.title: Sesame Street
results.brief_description:
Sesame Street first went to air in 1969. Created by the Children’s Television Workshop, it helped young children prepare for school. The Muppets were the key to the show’s success. During testing, children paid much more attention when Muppets were on screen, so producers eventually used them in every scene to keep the interest of their young viewers.

Characters like Bert and Ernie were intentionally simple in design and personality, making them easy to understand. The show also invited children to perform with The Muppets, often in improvised scenes, to talk about a problem or topic. The Muppets’ performances were so believable, that for their child co-stars, the crew working on set, and for everyone watching at home, they were treated and accepted as real. 

Sesame Street made learning feel like play, while helping children better understand friendship, families and feelings, as well as difficult issues like grief and discrimination. Versions of Sesame Street are currently broadcast in over 150 countries across the world.

results.credit_line: Courtesy Center for Puppetry Arts, Atlanta, USA
results.brief_description:
Brad is Bert’s nephew, who looks a lot like him.

Puppet has mustard yellow Antron fleece exterior and a tuft of orange faux fur hair on top of the head. Facial features include white eyes with black felt pupils, black faux fur unibrow, bulbous orange nose, and three jagged teeth in mouth. Costume includes white ribbed turtleneck with green patterned long sleeve shirt over the top and solid green pants. Shoes are greyish brown sueded material with white
laces.

results.title: The Muppet Show
results.brief_description:
Despite the success of Sesame Street, it took several years for Jim Henson to find a primetime home for a new set of characters with bigger egos and sharper jokes aimed at older audiences. In 1976, The Muppet Show premiered and was a hit across the globe almost immediately.

Each episode worked like a backstage comedy, where Kermit the Frog tried to keep the show running while everything went wrong around him. Major celebrities like Elton John, Diana Ross, Julie Andrews and Steve Martin joined The Muppets for sketches and songs, but the real stars were the chaotic puppets themselves. The main characters were featured in Time Magazine and interviewed on chat shows; taking on a life of their own beyond The Muppet Show.

The Muppets were messy, silly and not always very good at show business. Often, they failed – but they supported each other and never gave up, making them even more loveable.

results.title: The Muppet Movies
results.brief_description:
In the late 1970s, Jim Henson began preparing to bring the now famous Muppets to the big screen. The ambitious storylines meant that The Muppets had to move from the TV studio into the real world; to drive cars, ride bikes, and perform increasingly difficult stunts. The Henson team often had to invent solutions from scratch, combining puppetry with engineering, camera tricks and careful teamwork. 

For The Muppet Movie (1979), Henson performed Kermit the Frog singing “The Rainbow Connection” from inside a tiny diving bell hidden underwater. For The Great Muppet Caper (1981), Henson’s son Brian helped make The Muppets ride bikes through marionette rigging and rods that held the radio-controlled bikes together.

For Miss Piggy’s swimming sequence, Frank Oz swam unaided with Miss Piggy, wearing a wetsuit the same colour as the swimming pool walls. Despite these difficult conditions, following months of preparation and testing, the results look effortless and magical.
